cards.title: What generative modelling is
cards.hook: Learn the distribution of the data, then sample new data from it.

formula: sample generation, outlier detection (cracks, scratches), debiasing
hidden factors (pose, lighting, scale, identity) that explain x
example: Audio mixer: we hear the final mix x but not the hidden controls (vocals, bass, tempo) = latent z.
cards.memory: x is what you see, z is why.
cards.trap: Generative ≠ supervised: the goal is the DATA distribution, not a label.
explain: A generative model learns what the data looks like overall (its distribution), so it can produce new examples that look real, or tell when something looks unusual.
Much of what you see is explained by a few hidden factors (latent variables z): pose, lighting, identity. Generators learn to turn z into data x.

cards.title: Autoencoders and VAEs
cards.hook: Compress to a small code z, then rebuild: a VAE makes that code a well-behaved distribution.
cards.visual:
AutoencoderVAE
Encoder outputsa point zμ and σ (a distribution)
Loss‖x − x̂‖²reconstruction + KL to N(0, I)
Sampling new datapoorgood (continuity + completeness)
Trick–z = μ + σ⊙ε
cards.memory: VAE = AE + Variance + a nudge toward the standard normal.
cards.trap: We can't backprop through random sampling, so ε carries the randomness instead.
explain: An autoencoder squeezes the input through a small bottleneck z (encoder) and tries to rebuild it (decoder). No labels needed: the input is its own target.

A VAE makes the encoder output a mean μ and spread σ instead of a single point, samples z from them, and adds a KL penalty that pulls these distributions toward a standard normal. That keeps the latent space smooth, so random samples decode into sensible new data.
Reparameterisation trick: write z = μ + σ·ε with random ε, so gradients can flow through μ and σ.

cards.title: GANs
cards.hook: A forger (G) and a detective (D) train each other.
cards.visual:
PlayerWantsObjective
Discriminator DD(real) ≈ 1, D(fake) ≈ 0max E[log D(x)] + E[log(1 − D(G(z)))]
Generator Gfool Dmin the same expression
Equilibriump_G = p_dataD(x) ≈ 0.5 everywhere
formula: alternate: train D, then train G with D fixed
example: Interpolating z_A → z_B through the trained generator gives smoothly changing faces (StyleGAN2).
cards.memory: Forger vs detective until the detective just guesses (0.5).
cards.trap: G never sees real data directly: it learns only through D's feedback.
explain: A GAN is a contest between a forger and a detective. The generator G turns random noise into fake samples; the discriminator D tries to tell real from fake.
D is trained to output ≈1 on real data and ≈0 on fakes; G is trained to make D call its fakes real. When G becomes perfect, D can only guess: D(x) ≈ 0.5.
Mode collapse: G finds one kind of sample that fools D and keeps producing only that, missing the variety in the real data.

tex.t: \min_G \max_D\; \mathbb E_{x\sim p_{\text{data}}}\big[\log D(x)\big] + \mathbb E_{z\sim p(z)}\big[\log\big(1 - D(G(z))\big)\big]

cards.title: Autoregressive and diffusion models
cards.hook: Build data one piece at a time, or carve it out of noise step by step.
cards.visual:
ModelStarts fromGenerates by
VAElatent zdecoder → image
GANnoise zgenerator → image
Autoregressiveearlier elementsnext element → repeat
DiffusionGaussian noisedenoise → repeat → image
example: Causal mask: 'Force' sees May, the, Force but not 'be'.
cards.memory: AR = Again and Again (one token at a time); Diffusion = Dust off the noise.
cards.trap: Causal masking makes TRAINING parallel, but generation stays sequential.
explain: Autoregressive models write one piece at a time: predict a distribution for the next token, sample it, append it, repeat (this is how GPT writes).

Diffusion models learn to remove noise. Training: add a random amount of noise to a real image and teach a network to predict that noise. Generation: start from pure noise and repeatedly remove a little predicted noise until an image appears.
